tagline: Hamlet roads connect mills, farm buildings and the Cuyahoga Valley landscape.
intro: Heritage Corridors of Bath winds past early homes, barns, cemeteries and mills. Ohio’s Department of Transportation includes it among the state’s scenic byways, describing roads that connect 19th-century hamlets in rolling terrain within an urbanized area. Historic structures, a nature preserve and a national park are part of that setting.

At Ghent, Yellow Creek powered several mills as early as 1815. Nearby, Connecticut farmer Jonathan Hale established his homestead after migrating to the Western Reserve in 1810. His house dates to 1825. The Western Reserve Historical Society opened the farm in 1958 after receiving the property from his descendant Clara Belle Ritchie.

Begin with Ghent at Granger and Cleveland-Massillon roads, then continue north toward Bath at Cleveland-Massillon and Ira roads. Hale Farm and Village brings the journey into Cuyahoga Valley National Park. Nearby Indigo Lake, accessible from Riverview Road, occupies a former gravel and sand pit.

moments.title: Ghent
moments.text: Yellow Creek powered several mills at Ghent as early as 1815. Several families had settled here by 1818, and a post office operated from 1858 until 1918. The community occupies the area of Granger and Cleveland-Massillon roads in central Bath Township.

moments.title: Hale Farm and Village
moments.text: Hale Farm combines Jonathan Hale’s original homestead with a recreated village whose buildings mostly came from elsewhere. Hale migrated from Connecticut to the Western Reserve in 1810, and the house was built in 1825. His descendant Clara Belle Ritchie passed the property to the Western Reserve Historical Society, which opened it in 1958. In the recreated village, Wheatfield, most interpreters explain their buildings while acknowledging the modern world. The site also demonstrates 19th-century trades, including glassblowing, blacksmithing, and candle, broom and brick making. The property lies within the boundaries of Cuyahoga Valley National Park.

moments.title: Indigo Lake
moments.text: Indigo Lake began as Gray’s Quarry, a gravel and sand pit. The National Park Service took responsibility for it in 1974 with the creation of Cuyahoga Valley National Recreation Area. Park personnel later filled the pit with water to create the lake. Natural springs in the immediate area sustain its water supply. The roughly triangular lake lies entirely within Cuyahoga Valley National Park. Riverview Road provides access by car, while the Ohio & Erie Canal Towpath Trail provides an approach on foot. Largemouth bass are among the fish species found in the lake.
